projection.content: Write an essay of about 330 words on the history of lighthouses. Plain paragraphs only: no title, headings or lists.

For more than two thousand years, lighthouses have stood where land meets sea and warned sailors of danger. The earliest guides were simple fires lit on hilltops or beaches so that ships could find a harbor at night. Homer's poems mention such beacons, and as trade grew across the Mediterranean, people began building permanent towers to raise the flames higher and make them visible from farther away.

The most famous of these early structures was the Pharos of Alexandria, finished around 280 BCE under the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt. It is thought to have stood more than one hundred meters tall, and it was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It guided ships into one of the busiest ports of antiquity for centuries until earthquakes finally brought it down in the Middle Ages. The Romans built lighthouses across their empire, from Ostia to Dover. The

tower at A Coruña in Spain, known as the Tower of Hercules, still operates today.

After Rome fell, lighthouse building slowed, but it picked up again as medieval trade revived. Italian city-states such as Genoa put up towers to protect their merchant fleets, and monks sometimes kept lights burning on dangerous coasts. These lights still relied on wood fires, coal or candles, which were dim and needed constant tending.

The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries changed lighthouses completely. Engineers like John Smeaton, who built the Eddystone Lighthouse in England, worked out how to make stone towers that could survive violent waves. In 1822 the French physicist Augustin Fresnel invented a lens that gathered light into powerful beams, so a modest flame could be seen dozens of kilometers away. Oil lamps gave way to kerosene and then electricity, and each lighthouse was

given its own pattern of flashes so sailors could tell one from another.

Keepers and their families often lived in these remote stations. They trimmed wicks, wound clockwork, and polished lenses through long, lonely nights. In the twentieth century, automation gradually replaced them, and satellite navigation later made many lights less essential. Even so, lighthouses still guide ships today and remain lasting symbols of safety and human watchfulness.
